assessment.nobel_worthiness: Changed how economists and policymakers understand technology, task content, trade exposure and wage inequality. The work combines a conceptual task framework with credible, register-style and local-labour-market identification. It has had very large influence on research and public debate.
assessment.attribution: Autor and Katz are central to the task and skill-biased change literature. Autor and Hanson are central to the trade-shock evidence. Katz also has a long record on wage structure. Dorn is a major collaborator but is left out of a three-name limit. Daron Acemoglu, who is not credited here, is also closely tied to the task framework, so attribution is not clean.
assessment.maturity: Foundational papers date from the 1990s to the early 2000s, and the trade-shock work from about 2013. Replication, extensions and critiques are now extensive, so the core findings are well tested.
uncertainties: Debate over how far the trade-shock estimates generalize.
Overlap with Acemoglu's work on tasks and automation, and with other prize-recognised labour economics.
Choice of three names among four credited.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework with nominal rigidities underpins modern monetary-policy analysis and central-bank practice. It has very high conceptual and practical influence, and it is the workhorse for studying inflation targeting and policy rules.
assessment.attribution: Credit is diffuse across eight names, so a three-name selection is difficult. Woodford supplied the integrated theory of policy, Gali the empirical and theoretical development, and Taylor the policy rule and rule-based thinking. Calvo, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Gertler and Smets all have strong claims.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature. The framework has been central for more than two decades and has been tested through several crises.
uncertainties: Attribution among a very large group of credited names.
Weaknesses of the framework exposed after 2008 and 2021-22.
Overlap with prior macroeconomics prizes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamic panel estimators are a pervasive tool in empirical economics, used across labour, growth, finance and industrial organisation. The contribution is methodological, with large and long-lasting practical effects on applied work.
assessment.attribution: Arellano-Bond (1991), Arellano-Bover and Blundell-Bond (1998) form a coherent set of closely linked contributions. Credit to this trio is relatively clean, though Anderson-Hsiao, Hansen and Holtz-Eakin, Newey and Rosen are antecedents.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with more than three decades of use and well understood limitations.
uncertainties: Weak-instrument and many-instrument concerns in applied use.
The committee may judge a pure econometric-technique prize to be narrower than a field-defining discovery.
Antecedents and the GMM literature more broadly.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Bayesian persuasion and information design opened a new area of information economics. It has spread to applications in markets, regulation, politics and platform design, and it connects to mechanism design and information theory.
assessment.attribution: Kamenica-Gentzkow (2011) is the origin of the persuasion model. Bergemann and Morris developed information design and robust-predictions foundations. Selecting three of four credited names involves a judgement. Gentzkow is also known for other work.
assessment.maturity: Intermediate. The core paper is about 15 years old, and the applications are still growing. It is probably mature enough to assess the idea but still developing.
uncertainties: Whether the theory has yet been confirmed by empirical or practical impact.
Which of the four credited names best reflects the origin and development.
Relation to earlier cheap-talk and signalling work.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Reframed the analysis of cross-country income differences around the efficiency of allocation of inputs across firms. It is a significant bridge between micro data and aggregate productivity and growth, with wide application and policy relevance.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh-Klenow (2009) is the key paper and is the clearest basis for credit. Restuccia-Rosenthal-Rogerson (2008) is a parallel contribution, but the longlist credits Restuccia without Rogerson, which makes a three-name set awkward.
assessment.maturity: Moderately mature, with an influential literature of more than 15 years. Measurement concerns remain.
uncertainties: Sensitivity of misallocation estimates to measurement error and model structure.
Co-credit with Rogerson, who is not listed.
Whether the framework identifies causal sources of misallocation or measures dispersion.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Created long-run, tax-record-based series on top incomes and wealth. This reshaped empirical and policy discussion of inequality and led to a substantial research programme. Impact is very large, though the contribution is largely measurement and synthesis, plus some contested interpretation.
assessment.attribution: Piketty-Saez is the clear origin of the top-income series, and Zucman extended the work to wealth and offshore holdings. Atkinson and Kuznets are important antecedents. Attribution to three names is reasonable but leaves out other important contributors.
assessment.maturity: Mature for top-income series, still developing for wealth and offshore estimates.
uncertainties: Methodological disputes over wealth-distribution and capital-income estimates.
Whether the committee prioritises measurement over identified causal mechanisms.
Zucman's relative recency.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Alternating-offer bargaining gave a tractable, widely used strategic foundation for bargaining and decentralised market trade. It is deeply embedded in theory, labour and search models, and in applied work on negotiation.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein (1982) is the main contribution. Rubinstein-Wolinsky links it to markets. Binmore and Ståhl are important parallel contributors, and Binmore is on the list. Attribution is reasonably clear for Rubinstein, less so beyond him.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature, with more than 40 years of influence.
uncertainties: Possible overlap with earlier game-theory prizes.
Whether the committee sees this as a single-prize contribution or as a part of broader game theory.
Credit to Binmore and Ståhl.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Brought adverse-selection theory to data and showed how to measure selection, moral hazard and welfare effects in insurance markets. It has direct policy implications for health insurance design. Methods and findings are credible and influential across fields.
assessment.attribution: Finkelstein and Einav are the leading empirical contributors, with Finkelstein's randomised-evaluation work especially significant. Salanie, with Chiappori, contributed to testing for asymmetric information, and Chiappori is not listed. Finkelstein's other work, for example on health care, could blur the topic.
assessment.maturity: Fairly mature. The key papers date from about 2000 to 2015 and have been replicated and extended.
uncertainties: Possible overlap with the Chiappori contribution.
Whether the committee sees it as a recognised discovery or as a body of applied work.
Selection of three of the credited names.
